results.title: FX trades after volatility shocks | Macrosynergy
results.content:
Title: FX trades after volatility shocks | Macrosynergy
Currency areas with negative external balances are – all other things equal – more vulnerable to financing shocks. Hence, the products of external balances-based “resilience scores” and volatility shocks are plausible indicators of “post-shock currency hazards”. An empirical analysis based on 28 currencies since 2000 shows that a most simple “post-shock currency hazard” measure has significantly helped predict subsequent short-term returns and would have added positive PnL to FX trading strategies, particularly in times of turbulence. Finally, we also calculate volatility shocks for a basket of baskets, i.e. a global cross-asset class basket that gives approximately equal weight to FX, equity, and credit. * **GXA**: The first method measures the volatility shocks based on percent changes of average volatility indices across the asset classes, which dampens asset class-specific vol changes through diversification (GXA). ## Post-vol shock currency hazard #. The hypothesized exchange rate impact of a volatility shock on subsequent FX trends (currency hazard) can most simply be approximated by the volatility shock times the resilience score. We call this product **post-vol shock currency hazard**. The below panel shows the estimated post shows (balanced) post-shock hazards for 28 global currency areas since 2000. * balanced post-vol shock hazard based on average cross-asset class shock,. * balanced post-vol shock hazard based on maximum cross-asset class shock,. * one-sided post-vol shock hazard based on average cross-asset class shock, and. * one-sided post-vol shock hazard based on maximum cross-asset class shock. For the balanced average shock hazard and for all periods that recorded non-zero volatility shocks correlation has indeed been positive and significantly so, for the whole sample and both for the 2000-2010 and 2011-2022 subperiods. All other post-shock hazard versions posted significant positive forward return correlations too, with the one-sided post-shock hazards actually producing higher coefficients (8-12%) than the balanced ones (5-7.5%). Weekly accuracy, i.e. the ratio of correctly predicted weekly returns since 2000 has been 51.6% for the balanced average post-shock hazard and the panel. A naïve PnL that simply takes FX forward positions in proportion to the post-shock hazard on a weekly basis would have produced Sharpe ratios between 0.32 and 0.55, with infrequent trading and rare positioning.

Policy Implications and Strategic Recommendations The findi ngs from this research carry critical implications for economic policymakers, financial Given the quantifiable market impact of tariff policies, the deployment of predictive econometric models can act as early warning systems to mitigate risk Governments contemplating tariff imposition should be acutely aware of the market consequences, particularly in terms of capital flight, investor sentiment, and foreign direct As shown in our model, tariffs of even modest magnitude can lead to measurable downturns in equity markets, with broader economic repercussions.
